title: What Happens to India's Economy If Gen Z Stops Buying Homes
excerpt: With 27% of Gen Z Indians leaning toward renting and housing affordability at a crossroads, a generational shift in homebuying patterns could ripple through banking, construction, and GDP growth.
body:
• A Knight Frank report found only 71% of Gen Z Indians prefer homeownership, compared to 80-82% of older generations, with 27% leaning toward renting
  • India’s average homebuyer age has dropped from 38 to 34 in six years, but soaring property prices are pushing young professionals toward rental alternatives
  • HDFC Capital is launching a rental platform, signaling institutional investors are adapting to a generation that may not follow traditional homebuying patterns

India’s real estate market has long been driven by a cultural and financial imperative: buy a home as soon as you can afford one. But a growing body of data suggests Gen Z — those born between 1997 and 2012 — may be breaking that pattern, raising questions about the broader economic consequences.

The Numbers Tell a Shifting Story

According to a Knight Frank report, 79% of Baby Boomers, 80% of Gen X, and 82% of Millennials favor homeownership in India. Among Gen Z, that figure drops to 71%, with a notable 27% leaning toward renting — nearly triple the rate of older generations.

The reasons are a mix of choice and compulsion. Soaring real estate prices, stagnant entry-level salaries, and the rise of remote work have made the traditional 20-to-30-year mortgage less appealing. Podcaster Raj Shamani captured the sentiment in a viral post: “Long-term milestones like buying a home feel entirely out of reach in this economy.”

At the same time, a survey by Basic Home Loan found that 74% of homes sold in India are now bought by people under 35, and the average homebuyer age has dropped from 38 to 34 years in six years. The picture is not one of universal retreat from homeownership — it is one of deepening polarization.

Why the Economy Should Pay Attention

Real estate accounts for roughly 7-8% of India’s GDP and is deeply intertwined with banking, construction, steel, cement, and dozens of downstream industries. A sustained shift away from homebuying among the next generation of earners could slow credit growth, reduce demand for construction materials, and weaken the multiplier effect that housing investment creates.

The rental market, while growing, does not generate the same economic ripple. Home loans drive bank lending portfolios; construction employs millions of low-skilled workers; and property transactions generate significant tax revenue for state governments through stamp duty and registration fees.

Institutional Investors Are Adapting

HDFC Capital, one of India’s largest affordable housing investors, is launching a rental platform aimed at young professionals — a quiet admission that the “build-to-sell” model is no longer the only viable strategy.

“Not everybody can buy a house and not everybody needs to buy a house. If renting is done professionally, there are enough people who will choose it.”

— Vipul Roongta, CEO, HDFC Capital

Developers in cities like Bengaluru are seeing millennial and Gen Z property purchases surge 30-45% year-over-year, but much of this is concentrated in the mid-to-premium segment. The affordable housing segment — the entry point for most first-time buyers — remains under pressure.

Flexibility Over Legacy

For many young Indians, the calculus has changed. Job mobility, the rise of hybrid work, and a preference for experiences over assets are reshaping priorities. A 27-year-old finance professional in Gurugram told The Ken that he chose to rent rather than lock up money for 20-30 years in a property, splitting time between the city and his hometown 90 minutes away.

Developers are responding with co-living spaces, studio apartments, and tech-enabled smart homes. According to Knight Frank, 52% of respondents prefer apartments, followed by studio units at 19%.

What Comes Next

India’s housing market is not collapsing — but it is bifurcating. Wealthier Gen Z buyers are entering earlier and buying bigger, while those at the median income level are deferring or opting out entirely. Whether this shift is temporary or structural will depend on wage growth, interest rates, and whether developers and policymakers can create housing products that match what this generation actually wants and can afford.
